procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.07.2018 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in CRMWP No. 16825 of 2018
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court was petitioned under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to quash an FIR against the appellant under Section 376 of the Penal Code, 1860. The High Court declined to quash the FIR.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, implying they overturned the High Court's decision.

directions: The impugned order dated 26.07.2018 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad is set aside.
The FIR and all further proceedings based thereon are quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court ought to have exercised its inherent power under Section 482, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for quashing the FIR against the appellant under Section 376, Penal Code, 1860.

facts: An FIR was registered against the appellant under Sections 376 (rape) and 313 (causing miscarriage without woman's consent) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
The appellant filed a petition in the High Court to quash the FIR, but the High Court dismissed it.
Subsequently, the investigating agency itself omitted the allegation of the offence under Section 313 IPC against the appellant.
This left only the allegation under Section 376 IPC remaining for consideration.
law: The High Court has inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), as well as power under Article 226 of the Constitution, to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of the court or to secure the ends of justice.
The nomenclature under which a petition is filed (e.g., Article 226 vs. Section 482) is irrelevant, as the court can treat the petition under the appropriate provision.
The principles laid down in cases like *State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal* provide guidelines for when this extraordinary power can be exercised.
application: The Supreme Court's decision hinged on the crucial fact that the allegation under Section 313 IPC had been dropped by the investigating agency.

The Court reasoned that with the omission of the Section 313 charge, there was "absolutely no prima facie case for proceeding further against the appellant on the allegation of commission of offence punishable under Section 376, IPC."
It determined that allowing the criminal proceedings to continue solely on the remaining allegation, in this specific factual context, constituted an abuse of the process of the court.
The Court found that this was a "befitting case" where the High Court should have exercised its inherent power to intervene and quash the proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred by not exercising its inherent power under Section 482 CrPC. It held that once the allegation under Section 313 IPC was dropped, there was no prima facie case to continue with the Section 376 charge, and doing so would be an abuse of the court's process. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and quashed the FIR and all subsequent proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court ought to have exercised its inherent power under Section 482, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for quashing the FIR against the appellant under Section 376, Penal Code, 1860.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court should have quashed the FIR using its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC.

It was contended that the investigation itself, which included the complainant's statement and medical reports, concluded that there was no evidence to support the allegations (specifically referencing an investigation for an offence under Section 313 IPC).
respondent_arguments: The respondents (the State and the complainant) argued against the quashing of the FIR, supporting the High Court's decision not to interfere.

It can be inferred that they argued that the allegations were serious enough to warrant a full investigation and trial, and that it was not a fit case for the High Court to exercise its extraordinary jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana and Ors. v. Bhajan Lal and Ors.
cases.principle: For the illustrative categories of cases where the High Court can exercise its extraordinary power under Article 226 or inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court ought to exercise its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash a First Information Report (FIR) and all subsequent proceedings in order to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
obiter: It may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in not exercising its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the FIR. After considering the factual situation of the case in light of established legal principles, the Court concluded that this was a fit case for quashing the proceedings, implying that the continuation of the criminal case would amount to an abuse of the process of the court.
legal_tests_applied:
The court applied the illustrative categories laid down in the case of State of Haryana and Ors. v. Bhajan Lal and Ors. to determine when the extraordinary power under Section 482 CrPC should be exercised. The specific categories referenced by the court as guiding principles were:
1. (3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.
2. (5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
3. (7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.
policy_considerations: The court's decision reinforces the legal policy that the inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC are to be used to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice. This power serves as a crucial check against the continuation of criminal proceedings that are baseless, malicious, or where the evidence collected fails to establish a prima facie case against the accused.
